title: Parametric Motion Graphs
summary: Each graph node represents a continuous parameterized motion space constructed by blending aligned examples. Offline sampling finds acceptable transition regions between spaces and stores interpolation structures; runtime queries synthesize a clip and a compatible linear-blend transition rather than merely replaying a discrete edge.
limitations: Smooth parameter spaces and suitable examples are required. An edge cannot represent a source space containing any motion unable to transition to the target; restricting transitions can miss user targets. Linear blending is not a contact-force or dynamics certificate.
method: Each graph node represents a continuous parameterized motion space constructed by blending aligned examples. Offline sampling finds acceptable transition regions between spaces and stores interpolation structures; runtime queries synthesize a clip and a compatible linear-blend transition rather than merely replaying a discrete edge.
conditions: User-selected action and continuous controls such as travel curvature, punch target, duck height, platform height, and current character state. Action-specific functions translate joystick requests into graph parameters; feasible transition bounds can constrain the requested target.
evaluation: Sections 5.1–5.2 demonstrate locomotion, mixed traversal, boxing, random walks, searches, and interactive control. The boxing graph has nine edges and takes about 7 minutes 40 seconds to construct; visual examples establish the demonstrated scope rather than measured unseen-composition generalization.
evidence_locator: §§3.1–3.3 (transition construction), §4 (runtime extraction), §§5.1–5.2 and Figures 6,10 (examples/timing), §6 (limitations).
data_split: Not applicable as a statistical train/test benchmark. Example-based authoring uses separate action collections; the general traversal graph organizes 256 examples and the boxing graph 275 examples into three nodes. No held-out subject or combination protocol is reported.
metrics: Transition similarity thresholds define acceptable edges. Reported engineering measurements include per-edge construction time (2–147 seconds), complete graph construction time, and storage below 50 KB; there is no modern FID or standardized quantitative naturalness score.

title: Motion Synthesis from Annotations
summary: Uses annotated action timelines and multiscale dynamic programming to assemble motion, including overlapping qualitative constraints.
limitations: Cannot invent frames or transitions absent from the database. Incompatible requirements trade annotation satisfaction against continuity, and smoothing may change duration. Painted labels do not supply unseen contact geometry or physical execution.
method: SVM-assisted labeling propagates sparse manual action annotations. Multiscale dynamic programming then selects motion blocks that match a requested timeline while minimizing discontinuity, followed by finer boundary and motion refinement.
conditions: User-painted positive, negative or unconstrained action labels on a timeline, plus optional timed pose, root-position and orientation constraints. Vocabulary is chosen by the animator rather than fixed natural-language task understanding.
evaluation: Sections 3–6 demonstrate combinations such as running with jumping or waving and enforced key poses. Coarse-to-fine optimization improves solutions interactively; examples test overlapping qualitative requirements rather than a controlled statistical generalization benchmark.
evidence_locator: Sections 2–3 (annotations/synthesis), 4–5 (search/smoothing), 6 (Results); Figures 1, 5–7.
data_split: Uses a small annotated motion database, approximately seven minutes in the reported annotation exercise. SVM annotation propagation uses a manually labeled subset with interactive corrections. No held-out actor/action-combination benchmark or train/test percentage is reported for synthesis.
metrics: Annotation matching and motion-continuity objectives, interactive synthesis behavior, visual naturalness and low-level constraint satisfaction. Annotation speed is demonstrated; no standardized distributional generation or independent physics metric is reported.

title: Interactive motion generation from examples
summary: Cuts and pastes mocap via randomized hierarchical graph search under constraints at interactive speeds.
limitations: Database coverage directly limits feasible actions. Randomized search is not a completeness guarantee, and visually acceptable transition costs do not establish physical consistency or arbitrary interaction synthesis.
method: Builds a directed graph over captured motion frames, with transitions scored by pose and velocity compatibility. A hierarchy clusters similar transition alternatives; randomized mutation searches coarse graph paths and progressively refines them into reusable clip sequences. Constraint costs guide selection, while blending and postprocessing address local discontinuities.
conditions: Animator specifies duration and timed body positions, orientation, joint states or whole-body poses. Coordinated characters can be constrained at interaction poses; this is explicit constraint authoring rather than language-conditioned generation.
evaluation: Section 5 reports acceptable 300-frame solutions in approximately 3–10 seconds on the stated Pentium III machine. Examples combine several source pieces and include constrained interactions; judgments are principally demonstrative rather than a controlled perceptual benchmark.
evidence_locator: Sections 3–4 (graph/hierarchical search), Section 5 (Results), Appendix A (transition cost).
data_split: No supervised train/validation/test partition applies to graph construction. Demonstrations use roughly 60–80 short motion recordings; scalability is discussed for databases of 50–100 motions. An independently held-out compositional test set is not reported.
metrics: Visual human-likeness, foot slipping/jerk inspection, constraint satisfaction, synthesis latency and graph preprocessing time; no FID, contact accuracy or statistical generalization metric.

title: Motion Graphs
summary: Builds a directed graph of captured clips and synthesized transitions; graph walks satisfy user constraints such as locomotion paths.
limitations: Transition thresholds require manual selection and can be laborious across diverse movements. Candidate comparison costs quadratically many frame pairs. Only nearby motions admit simple reliable blends; sparse connectivity and source-library coverage bound possible behaviors. Demonstrations do not establish unseen task composition or object-aware manipulation.
method: Constructs a directed graph whose edges are captured motion fragments and synthesized transitions. Candidate connections minimize aligned point-cloud distances over temporal windows, with floor-plane translation/yaw factored out. Locally similar windows are blended, constraint labels are propagated, and problematic graph portions are pruned. Branch-and-bound graph search then minimizes an application-specific additive objective; footplant constraints can be enforced after extraction.
conditions: A captured motion database, optional action/constraint labels, a desired planar path, and restrictions on action types along portions of the path.
evaluation: Section 5 demonstrates walking, sneaking, martial arts and constrained changes between these styles. A 12.8-second sneaking capture plus its mirror yields alternative paths. The walking Hello example needs 58.1 seconds computation for 54.9 seconds animation.
data_split: No learned train/validation/test split: demonstrations reuse a finite motion library. Largest example has approximately 6,000 frames/200 seconds; other graphs contain about 3,000 frames.
metrics: Path-fitting objective measures deviation between requested and synthesized paths. Reports construction/search wall time and animation duration; no FID, semantic retrieval benchmark, or statistical user-study score.

title: PRISM: Per-unit Kinematic Motion Generation in a Structured Latent Manifold
summary: The inspected revision uses a causal temporal VAE with separate kinematic-unit latent tokens, a joint/time structured flow generator, kinematic-tree rotary positional encoding, and depth-dependent flow sampling. A clean-context mask provides prefix continuation and successive segment generation with one frozen generator.
limitations: The current PDF is retitled PRISM: Per-Unit Kinematic Motion Generation in a Structured Latent Manifold, so earlier streaming-title claims need revision alignment. SMPL body coverage excludes expressive hands/face; full object-conditioned interaction and dynamics are not evaluated.
publication_note: The inspected v4 PDF is retitled from "PRISM: Streaming Human Motion Generation with Per-Joint Latent Decomposition". The official BibTeX endpoint still returns that earlier title; this record transcribes the v4 title page and pins the citation to v4.
method: The inspected revision uses a causal temporal VAE with separate kinematic-unit latent tokens, a joint/time structured flow generator, kinematic-tree rotary positional encoding, and depth-dependent flow sampling. A clean-context mask provides prefix continuation and successive segment generation with one frozen generator.
conditions: Text and optional clean initial pose frames; long narratives are decomposed into ordered captions and durations shared across compared generators. The evaluated prefix lengths are 1, 5, and 9 frames. Arbitrary body-part or scattered-frame control is explicitly future work.
evaluation: Tables I–IV compare text generation, prefix conditioning, BABEL episodes, and reconstruction; matched 1D/2D, positional-encoding, and sampler ablations isolate design choices. Narrative outputs use frozen common plans and tie-aware ranking. This is paper-reported evidence, not an independent rerun.
evidence_locator: §III (causal kinematic-unit VAE, KU-FlowT, KT-RoPE, KAFS), §IV.A–G and Tables I–VIII; Appendix A shared TMR protocol and Appendix B narrative composition/user-study setup; §VI limitations.
data_split: Trained on approximately 200,000 public MotionHub SMPL(-X) motion-text pairs; evaluates the HumanML3D split and FlowMDM BABEL protocol, plus 50 narratives in 10 categories containing 4–10 actions. Exact training-source group proportions are not reported in the inspected experimental description.
metrics: TMR-based R-Precision and MM-Distance measure semantic correspondence; FID measures feature-distribution differences; Diversity measures variability. BABEL transition FID evaluates boundaries. Shared-skeleton slide, float, and jitter errors probe kinematic artifacts; narrative rankings measure human preferences.

title: Streaming Multi-Track Timeline Control for 3D Human Motion Generation
summary: TimelineControl combines interval-aware conditioning, causal part representations and part-aware denoising with TimelineMotion annotations.
limitations: Synthetic compositional references inherit source and stitching biases. Demonstrated streaming alignment is bounded by evaluated instructions; humanoid examples do not establish general autonomous manipulation or independent physical certification.
method: Combines interval-aware instruction encoding with causal, anatomically factored motion features and a part-aware streaming denoiser. Instruction tokens retain their start/end times; learned body-part relevance biases cross-attention. The TimelineMotion construction stitches compatible HumanML3D clips with STMC, then refines boundaries and filters abrupt translation or jitter.
conditions: Incrementally received text instructions with overlapping intervals and body-part relevance; optional spatial targets. Future instructions unavailable at a streaming instant are excluded from conditioning.
evaluation: Compares offline STMC and streaming baselines, including ActionPlan retrained on matching data. Tables 1–4 isolate interval conditioning, skeletal structure, part bias and denoising branches; Appendix C checks temporal-score sensitivity to shifted intervals.
evidence_locator: Sections 4.1–4.4; Sections 5.1–5.4, Tables 1–4; Appendices A and C (data/protocol).
data_split: TimelineMotion contains 44,944 synthetic sequences. Source clips for each timeline come from the same HumanML3D partition, preserving its split membership. Evaluates TimelineMotion and MTT test sets plus HumanML3D; exact partition proportions are not restated in the inspected protocol.
metrics: TMR R-Precision, motion-to-text similarity M2T, source similarity M2M, FID/FID+, transition distance, Temporal AP and ROC-AUC for interval adherence; human preference and control-target errors.

title: DartControl: A Diffusion-Based Autoregressive Motion Model for Real-Time Text-Driven Motion Control
summary: Latent diffusion predicts motion primitives from history and current text; noise optimization or RL provides spatial control.
limitations: Short local history and a kinematic generative prior do not certify physical execution. HumanML3D subset differences matter for comparison. Goal-reaching results concern the demonstrated control setup, not general dexterous object manipulation or arbitrary scene-task completion.
method: Learns a history-conditioned motion-primitive VAE and text/history-conditioned latent diffusion model. Each primitive contains two history frames and eight generated frames, canonicalized around the pelvis. Scheduled autoregressive training mitigates rollout mismatch. Spatial control operates through latent-noise optimization, or a separately trained reinforcement-learning policy whose actions select latent noise; this differs from training a physics-based low-level humanoid controller.
conditions: An initial motion seed, an ordered stream of text prompts with durations, and optional goals, trajectories or scene geometry for the chosen control application.
evaluation: Compares TEACH, DoubleTake, history-conditioned T2M-GPT and FlowMDM; profiles 5,000-frame generation and conducts perceptual comparisons. Optimization and RL goal-reaching are evaluated separately.
evidence_locator: Sections 3.1–3.3, 4.1–4.3; Tables 1–4; Appendices B, E and G.
publication_note: First public preprint 2024. First public preprint 2024.
data_split: BABEL training recordings train the default model; temporal composition evaluates its released validation set because its test set is unavailable. HumanML3D experiments use only records with available SMPL motion, excluding joint-only/mirrored sources; exact retained counts are not given in Appendix B.
metrics: FID, R-precision, MM-DIST and diversity assess segments; peak jerk and area under jerk assess 30-frame transition windows. Also reports latency, frames/second, memory, reach time/success, foot skating and foot-floor distance.

title: Motion Mamba: Efficient and Long Sequence Motion Generation
summary: Motion Mamba replaces expensive denoising sequence operations with state-space blocks. Hierarchical Temporal Mamba varies temporal scan depth across the U-shaped network, while Bidirectional Spatial Mamba scans pose features in both directions to couple spatial channels and temporal dependencies.
limitations: The long-sequence experiment concerns single-description benchmark clips and cannot establish arbitrary multi-prompt temporal composition. Motion-feature scores and short generation latency do not establish contact correctness, scene compatibility, or full-body physical executability.
method: Motion Mamba replaces expensive denoising sequence operations with state-space blocks. Hierarchical Temporal Mamba varies temporal scan depth across the U-shaped network, while Bidirectional Spatial Mamba scans pose features in both directions to couple spatial channels and temporal dependencies.
conditions: Natural-language embeddings condition a diffusion motion generator; sequence duration follows benchmark generation settings. This is a text-to-motion backbone, without an explicit ordered action schedule, object mesh, scene map, or manipulation contact constraints as core input.
evaluation: Tables 1–2 benchmark HumanML3D and KIT-ML, Table 3 tests the long-sequence slice, and Table 4 ablates temporal scans, spatial scans, latent size, and depth. Qualitative examples and a user study supplement numerical and speed comparisons.
evidence_locator: §3 and Figure 2 (HTM/BSM architecture), §§4.1–4.5, Tables 1–4, Figure 4 (V100 latency).
data_split: HumanML3D and KIT-ML follow the standard text-motion evaluation protocol. The paper does not restate exact train/validation/test proportions in §4.1. HumanML3D-LS selects original evaluation motions longer than 190 frames; this is a length slice, not a held-out action-combination split.
metrics: FID measures learned motion-feature distribution mismatch; R-Precision and MM-Distance measure text-motion alignment; Diversity and Multimodality measure overall and same-prompt variation. Average inference time measures latency on a single V100. Evaluations repeat 20 times with 95% confidence intervals.

title: Multi-Track Timeline Control for Text-Driven 3D Human Motion Generation
summary: Test-time spatial stitching and temporal score arithmetic operate at every diffusion step.
method: Preprocesses prompts into per-body-part timelines; denoises local crops and combines corresponding pose components repeatedly during sampling.
conditions: Multiple texts with explicit time intervals and body-part assignments, supplied manually or inferred with GPT-3. Compatible overlapping part responsibilities are required; the motion is jointly assembled at every denoising step.
evaluation: Table 1 compares single-text, single-track and multi-track sampling with several denoisers. A filtered pairwise human study evaluates one hundred motions for realism and instruction adherence. Improvements are evaluated separately for semantics and transitions, avoiding an aggregate claim of physical correctness. The composition procedure updates all local denoising crops repeatedly rather than stitching final outputs once.
limitations: Inherits base-model failures, unfamiliar stitched poses and imperfect timing. Incompatible parts remain problematic; long-motion TMR embeddings are unreliable, motivating cropped FID+. Contact mechanics and persistent object state are not modeled.
evidence_locator: Sections 3.1–3.4, 4.1–4.6; Table 1 and user-study protocol.
data_split: Backbone models train on HumanML3D. MDM-SMPL excludes HumanAct12 because pose parameters are unavailable. MTT is a manually designed evaluation-only timeline set with atomic text/source-motion references; no newly trained timeline partition or train/test percentage applies to STMC itself.
metrics: TMR R@1/R@3, motion-to-text M2T and motion-to-motion M2M similarity; FID+ uses five random five-second crops per generated timeline, and transition distance measures local consecutive-pose boundary jumps.

title: Seamless Human Motion Composition with Blended Positional Encodings
summary: FlowMDM generates temporally composed text-conditioned motion and evaluates transition quality.
limitations: Finite attention and independent low-frequency subsequence structure can limit distant action relationships. Good jerk or FID values do not establish semantic task prerequisites, foot-support correctness, scene collision freedom or object interaction dynamics.
method: Early denoising uses absolute positions for within-action structure; late denoising uses relative positions across boundaries. Pose-centric cross-attention associates each frame with its own condition.
conditions: Ordered text descriptions and durations, expanded to frame-specific conditions. Pose-centric cross-attention associates each frame with its own prompt while the denoising process changes positional-encoding regime.
evaluation: Tables 1–2 compare TEACH, DoubleTake, DiffCollage and MultiDiffusion with matched conditioning/positional choices. Thirty-one transitions between the thirty-two subsequences are evaluated separately; ablations examine positional blending, attention horizon and pose-centric conditioning. Extrapolation tests extend beyond training sequence durations.
evidence_locator: Sections 3.1–3.3, 4.1–4.4; Tables 1–2; Eq. 4 for PJ/AUJ and supplementary evaluation details.
data_split: Uses the standard BABEL and HumanML3D training/test divisions; exact partition proportions are not restated in Section 4.1. BABEL training may include consecutive annotated actions; HumanML3D lacks explicit transition annotations. Evaluation composes thirty-two sampled text-duration pairs per long sequence.
metrics: Subsequence R-Precision, matching distance, FID, diversity/multimodality; transition FID, Peak Jerk PJ and Area Under the Jerk AUJ quantify both abrupt spikes and excessive broad smoothing.

title: T2LM: Long-Term 3D Human Motion Generation from Multiple Sentences
summary: Uses a local 1D-convolutional VQ-VAE decoder to decode a continuous text-predicted latent stream, trained on short clips.
limitations: Local continuity does not enforce scene/contact correctness or long-range task causality. Standard feature metrics depend on their learned representation; ST2M is excluded because motion representations differ, preventing direct score equivalence.
method: Trains a convolutional VQ-VAE whose local temporal receptive fields map motion to a stream of discrete codes. A text-conditioned predictor learns codes from short clips. At inference, multiple sentence-conditioned latent subsequences are assembled and decoded together, allowing local decoder neighborhoods to produce transitions without training on long sequential demonstrations.
conditions: Ordered sentence list and requested segment durations; outputs continuous skeletal motion. The method does not receive an object mesh, scene occupancy or future object-state supervision.
evaluation: Tables 4–5 compare long sequences with DoubleTake, TEACH and MultiAct; Tables 6–7 assess single actions. Codebook and explicit transition-latent ablations test representation choices. The paper reports weaker transition-scope performance than TEACH on BABEL despite stronger overall-window quality.
evidence_locator: Sections 3, 4.2–4.5; Tables 2–7; discussion following Table 5.
data_split: Trains/evaluates on HumanML3D and BABEL following their cited standard protocols. The paper distinguishes short-clip training from sequential evaluation; exact split proportions and actor-disjointness are not specified in its dataset subsection.
metrics: R-Precision, FID, MM-Distance, Diversity and reconstruction FID; sliding-scope SS-FID/SS-Diversity and transition-scope TS-FID/TS-Diversity use 80-frame windows, with a 40-frame stride for sliding evaluation.

title: AMD: Autoregressive Motion Diffusion
summary: Introduces HumanLong3D and conditions iterative diffusion generation on current text plus previous text and action sequences.
limitations: Longer rollout depends on generated context and can accumulate error. A dataset-example split does not establish unseen skill-pair or actor generalization. Online estimated dance poses and newly collected motion have different provenance and should not be treated as uniform measured ground truth.
method: Autoregressively generates one diffusion-based motion segment per ordered text prompt. A context encoder combines the current prompt, the preceding prompt and preceding generated motion; a duration network predicts a categorical distribution over segment lengths. Training couples temporal motion context and denoising, rather than independently synthesizing clips and interpolating them afterward. The paper also builds HumanLong3D with coherence annotations and HumanMusic from online dance videos.
conditions: Ordered natural-language prompts and prior generated segment context; a music-conditioned variant uses audio features. Segment duration is predicted rather than assumed fixed at deployment.
evaluation: Compares joint prediction, independent generation/interpolation and autoregressive prediction on HumanLong3D, alongside short text-to-motion baselines. The duration network covers approximately 2–9.8 seconds per segment in the implementation.
evidence_locator: Our Approach; Datasets and Evaluation Metrics; Comparisons on Compound Motion; Tables 1–3; Figure 1.
data_split: HumanLong3D compound-motion experiment partitions examples into training/test/validation at 85/10/5 percent. Exact subject, source-recording or composition-ancestor separation is not specified. HumanML3D provides the short-motion benchmark; AIST++ and HumanMusic provide music experiments.
metrics: FID measures generated/reference feature-distribution distance; top-3 R-precision and multimodal distance measure text alignment; diversity and multimodality measure across-prompt and within-prompt variation. Music evaluation follows the cited dance protocol.

title: DiffCollage: Parallel Generation of Large Content with Diffusion Models
summary: DiffCollage represents large content through a factor graph of overlapping smaller regions. It combines local diffusion scores with overlap corrections to approximate a global score, allowing the regions to denoise concurrently. The same construction is applied to images and long human motion.
limitations: The factorization approximates the full distribution and depends on informative overlaps. Cropped feature metrics do not prove global ordering, distant consistency, collision freedom, or valid hand-object contact. The motion results should remain distinct from its stronger image-generation evaluation coverage.
method: DiffCollage represents large content through a factor graph of overlapping smaller regions. It combines local diffusion scores with overlap corrections to approximate a global score, allowing the regions to denoise concurrently. The same construction is applied to images and long human motion.
conditions: Pretrained short-content diffusion models and a chosen factor graph; motion factors may carry different text prompts. Overlap structure determines how local constraints communicate, while optional inpainting conditions preserve specified content. It is a sampling composition method rather than a new motion-capture dataset.
evaluation: §5.2 and Table 3 compare parallel factor-graph generation with naive long denoising and autoregressive replacement/reconstruction. Multiple-action demonstrations provide qualitative prompt composition; image experiments additionally test panorama generation, inpainting, and latency scaling.
evidence_locator: §§3–4 (factor graphs and score assembly), §5.2, Table 3 and motion-composition examples; appendix implementation details.
data_split: Motion experiments use the HumanML3D test set with an existing short-motion model. Long outputs are 24 seconds, approximately four times average training duration. Exact source-model train/validation proportions are not restated; image experiments additionally use internal landscapes, LHQ, and LSUN Tower.
metrics: R-Precision and multimodal distance assess text-motion alignment, FID measures distribution mismatch, and Diversity measures variability. Long-motion evaluation randomly crops generated sequences for short-motion evaluators, so its scores characterize local windows rather than complete narrative correctness.

title: Human Motion Diffusion as a Generative Prior
summary: Introduces DoubleTake sequential composition, ComMDM two-person coordination and DiffusionBlending joint-control model composition.
limitations: DoubleTake needs overlap/refinement design; ComMDM needs interaction data and fine control requires extra training. These are distinct reuse mechanisms, not a universal zero-training composer. None guarantees physically valid contact or persistent object-state reasoning.
method: A frozen short-motion diffusion prior is reused for overlapping prompted intervals; a second take refines transitions. Separate small adapters or fine-tuned controlled priors support other composition modes.
conditions: DoubleTake consumes sequential prompts/durations with overlapping handshake regions. ComMDM additionally consumes interaction examples or a prefix; fine-tuned priors consume selected joint controls, and DiffusionBlending combines distinct control-conditioned predictions.
evaluation: Sequential evaluation constructs thirty-two-interval sequences and scores actions and boundaries separately. ComMDM completes three seconds from a one-second prefix and compares communication-layer placement. Fine-tuning and blending compare a common initial MDM against separately controlled models.
evidence_locator: Sections 3.1–3.3, 4.1–4.3; Tables 1–3 and fine-control quantitative results.
publication_note: First public preprint; conference publication 2024. First public preprint; conference publication 2024.
data_split: DoubleTake evaluates BABEL and HumanML3D; fine control uses HumanML3D test prompts/controls. ComMDM uses a small two-person dataset, including its ten-example few-shot setting. Exact aggregate train/test proportions are not restated and the three tasks should not be collapsed into one split.
metrics: Per-interval text-motion R-Precision/MM-Distance/FID/diversity, transition FID; ComMDM prefix completion reports root/joint L2 errors. Joint-control evaluation measures adherence and generation quality; qualitative studies assess blending.

title: Sequential Texts Driven Cohesive Motions Synthesis with Natural Transitions
summary: Combines previous/current text semantics with learnable transition tokens and a transition loss.
limitations: Endpoint distance measures boundary jumps rather than natural braking, support transfer or continuous collision freedom. Synthetic sequences and a custom paired feature extractor complicate comparison with methods using different BABEL representations.
method: Uses semantic fusion attention to combine current sentence features with preceding motion context. A transformer infers learnable starting transition snippet codes from the previous generated motion; an autoregressive generator then continues the current action. A dedicated transition loss encourages continuity. STDM is synthesized to supply longer sequential text-motion examples.
conditions: Sequential text descriptions, generated previous motion/snippet context, and sequence lengths. Historical semantics are learned rather than treating each sentence as an independent clip.

title: MultiAct: Long-Term 3D Human Motion Generation from Multiple Action Labels
summary: Recurrently conditions on prior motion and the next action label to generate transitions and long multi-action sequences.
limitations: Discrete action categories provide less detailed control than text or geometry. Recurrent generation is assessed on BABEL’s annotated transitions, and favorable feature scores do not certify foot contact, object consistency, or arbitrary physical task sequencing.
year_basis: First public preprint in December 2022; revised 2023.
method: MultiAct recurrently predicts a transition and next action through MACVAE, a motion-and-action-conditioned variational autoencoder. Separate latent variables encode the previous-motion context and current action. A face-front canonicalization removes heading and location while retaining the gravity relationship, avoiding the floor-orientation loss caused by full root zeroing. An ACTOR model produces the initial action before recurrent continuation.
conditions: A sequence of discrete action labels and previous generated motion; transition and action durations are part of the sampled training/generation setting, not free-form language understanding.
evaluation: Compares MACVAE to action-conditioned generation combined with interpolation or a motion-transition model. Ablations remove separate latents and vary canonicalization or previous-motion input; long-horizon plots track action accuracy and transition distribution.
evidence_locator: MACVAE and Long-Term Motion Generation sections; Datasets; Evaluation metrics; Tables 1–3; Figures 4–6.
publication_note: First public preprint in December 2022; revised 2023. First public preprint in December 2022; revised 2023.
data_split: Uses BABEL training split for learning and released validation split for testing, extracting alternating action and transition intervals. Test previous-motion inputs are unseen examples; no independently held-out action-pair split or new proportional split is declared in the main paper.
metrics: FID against training and test feature distributions, top-1/top-5 action recognition, diversity across actions and multimodality within actions. Transition FID and action accuracy are also measured along long rollouts.

title: TEACH: Temporal Action Composition for 3D Humans
summary: TEACH extends a text-motion variational Transformer with past-motion conditioning: it generates all frames of one action non-autoregressively, then conditions the next action on a short history. Training on adjacent action pairs teaches continuity; alignment and spherical interpolation further smooth transitions.
limitations: Pairwise BABEL supervision and validation-set reporting limit claims about unseen independent recordings and new action combinations. Autoregressive rollout can accumulate errors, while interpolation does not establish scene feasibility or contact-rich manipulation. Position-based comparison to one reference underestimates valid alternative realizations.
method: TEACH extends a text-motion variational Transformer with past-motion conditioning: it generates all frames of one action non-autoregressively, then conditions the next action on a short history. Training on adjacent action pairs teaches continuity; alignment and spherical interpolation further smooth transitions.
conditions: An ordered list of action descriptions, individual action durations, and the previous generated action tail. The main configuration uses five past frames. The model generates body motion and root displacement, without receiving manipulated object meshes or object-state trajectories.
evaluation: Table 1 compares independent, jointly generated, and past-conditioned action pairs; Table 2 tests alignment/interpolation and transition distances; Table 3 varies past-context length. Qualitative longer chains test repeated action-level rollout beyond pairwise training.

title: FUSION: Full-Body Unified Motion Prior for Body and Hands via Diffusion
summary: Unifies body and hand datasets into a full-body motion prior, with optimization-driven object-motion and self-interaction applications.
limitations: Randomly combined hand/body motion lacks sequence-level semantic correlation. Fixed-grasp guidance limits contact changes, and the learned prior is not a text-plus-initial-state dynamic HOI generator. Body-only realism scores cannot validate dexterous hand or object dynamics.
method: Unconditional SMPL-X diffusion prior jointly models body/hands; task losses backpropagate through denoising to optimize noise. Local hand transfer preserves body wrists and filters additional penetration.
conditions: Unconditional whole-body/hand prior optimized for supplied keypoint tracks, object-motion trajectories or LLM-generated timed self-contact constraints. Object-guided synthesis assumes object motion and a stable grasp, so future interaction is partially prescribed.
evaluation: Keypoint control is compared with TLControl; hand/body ablations assess the benefit of unified training. Object-guided and self-interaction demonstrations optimize denoising noise with task losses. Human comparison separately assesses motion realism against HMP and captured motion.
evidence_locator: Sections 3.1–3.3, 4–5; Table 1; supplementary Sections 9–12 (metrics, ablations, self-contact).

ARCTIC/GRAB test sources and task-specific test conditions are described, but aggregate source-ancestor split grouping is not fully enumerated.

title: MixerMDM: Learnable Composition of Human Motion Diffusion Models
summary: Learns adversarial dynamic mixing of pretrained single-person and interaction diffusion models.
limitations: Requires additional training and inference computation, adversarial stability tuning and compatible output representations. Mixing model distributions does not construct a provenance-preserving human-object dataset or prove unseen action-order generalization.

conditions: Interaction-level text plus per-person text descriptions and the two pretrained diffusion predictions at each denoising step. Tests interchangeable interaction/individual backbones.

metrics: Alignment applies Top-3 R-Precision separately to individual and interaction conditions; Adaptability measures variation under individual condition changes. Human-study average rank/first-place rate supplement feature-based evaluation.

title: SALAD: Skeleton-aware Latent Diffusion for Text-driven Motion Generation and Editing
summary: Models joint-frame-word relationships and edits generated motion by cross-attention modulation without explicit user masks.
limitations: Diversity remains limited and competes with fidelity. Only a single person and bounded text/motion lengths are modeled. The authors explicitly state that editing real recorded motions is not directly addressed; attention preservation ratings are not an exact frame/joint invariance guarantee.
method: Trains a skeleto-temporal VAE with skeletal pooling and temporal compression, preserving joint/frame structure in latent space. A denoiser separately models skeletal, temporal and word-level relations. At inference, cross-attention maps support word swapping, attention reweighting and left/right attention mirroring without training a dedicated editor or requiring an explicit edit mask.
conditions: Natural-language descriptions and requested sequence length; editing manipulates the attention of a source generation using changed words or weights, rather than directly accepting arbitrary captured motion.
evaluation: Table 1 averages 20 evaluations with 95 percent confidence intervals. Compares generation with diffusion/token baselines and editing with MDM and MotionFix; ablates guidance, parameterization, VAE and FiLM components.

title: ParCo: Part-Coordinating Text-to-Motion Synthesis
summary: Separate part tokenizers and lightweight generators communicate through a coordination module.
limitations: Six-part factorization alone is not evidence of arbitrary simultaneous semantic composition. Evaluator training-distribution bias can make generated samples outperform real test motions; semantic accuracy and physical validity need complementary checks.
method: Partitions a skeleton into six anatomical streams and learns separate part VQ tokenizers. Lightweight autoregressive text-conditioned generators predict part tokens while a coordination module exchanges information between streams. Their decoders reconstruct a unified whole-body sequence; this reduces whole-body token complexity while preserving inter-part dependencies.
conditions: A natural-language motion description; variable output duration is predicted autoregressively rather than supplied as ground-truth length. Part streams are internal representations, not independent user-assigned task labels.

data_split: HumanML3D and KIT-ML use the cited standard train/validation/test divisions. Numerical proportions are not restated. A diagnostic additionally divides HumanML3D test captions into four approximately equal length quartiles, not four independent training splits.
metrics: R-Precision Top-1/2/3, FID, multimodal distance, diversity and multimodality, computed with the established pretrained text-motion evaluator. Diagnostic left/right instruction tests and caption-length subsets supplement these scores.

title: BAMM: Bidirectional Autoregressive Motion Model
summary: Bidirectional autoregressive motion-token generation predicts ending and supports completion and long-sequence synthesis.
limitations: Long composition and editing are broader applications than the core single-caption quantitative benchmark. Learned feature scores do not measure object contact, task-order causality or continuous physical feasibility, and duration conditions must match for fair comparisons.
method: Encodes motion with a residual vector quantizer, then learns a masked bidirectional autoregressive transformer over token sequences. conditions: Text, optionally specified motion length, and motion tokens retained as editing/completion constraints. Long composition chains prompts through constrained generation rather than learning explicit object-state transitions.

title: MotionFix: Text-Driven 3D Human Motion Editing
summary: MotionFix mines semantically related source/target motion pairs with a retrieval model and collects human instructions describing the change. TMED learns conditional diffusion over the target using separate source-motion and text encodings, with independently dropped conditions enabling dual-condition classifier-free guidance.
limitations: One valid target is not the unique correct realization of an instruction, and embedding retrieval does not separately guarantee preservation of every unchanged detail. Random triplet splitting should not be read as independent-person generalization. No mesh-conditioned interaction or dynamics benchmark is claimed.
method: MotionFix mines semantically related source/target motion pairs with a retrieval model and collects human instructions describing the change. TMED learns conditional diffusion over the target using separate source-motion and text encodings, with independently dropped conditions enabling dual-condition classifier-free guidance.
conditions: A complete source motion and natural-language editing instruction; source and target can have different durations. The model learns edit relationships from explicit triplets rather than treating a new action description as equivalent to an instruction about a supplied motion.
evaluation: Section 5 compares TMED with text-motion-only baselines, body-part inpainting, and source initialization approaches. Data-size and condition-guidance ablations examine the value of paired editing supervision; qualitative edits show changed speed, direction, posture, or repetition.
evidence_locator: §3 (pair mining/annotation and 5387/330/1013 partition), §4 (TMED and guidance), §§5.1–5.3 (retrieval protocol, comparisons, ablations).
data_split: The dataset contains 6,730 triplets and is randomly partitioned into 5,387 training, 330 validation, and 1,013 test triplets, described as 80/5/15%. The paper specifies triplet-level random splitting; it does not claim a cross-subject or source-recording-disjoint evaluation.
metrics: Motion-to-motion retrieval ranks the reference target against candidates using learned embeddings; top-K recall and average rank assess target proximity. The rank of the source indicates how much the output changes, but high source similarity alone is not successful editing.

title: MMM: Generative Masked Motion Model
summary: Text-conditioned masked motion tokens support in-betweening, body-part changes and long sequence synthesis.
limitations: Fine details for exceptionally long single descriptions remain difficult because training motions reach at most about 196 frames. The model does not support multi-person interactions. method: Learns a VQ motion tokenizer with an 8,192-entry factorized codebook, then trains a text-conditioned transformer to reconstruct randomly masked tokens. Iterative parallel decoding retains confident tokens and remasks uncertain ones. Arbitrary temporal masks enable in-betweening; long generation first synthesizes prompt-specific segments and fills transition tokens. Upper-body editing uses separately pretrained upper/lower tokenizers and specialized conditioning rather than arbitrary joint editing in the default whole-body tokenizer.
conditions: Text prompts, requested motion length, and optional visible motion tokens or an upper/lower-body editing partition.
evaluation: Quantitative generation evaluation repeats 20 times with 95 percent confidence intervals. Tables 1–2 compare benchmark generation; timing uses the same RTX A5000. Qualitative comparisons show in-betweening, upper-body replacement and sequential stories, with masking/iteration ablations.

data_split: HumanML3D and KIT-ML use motion-sequence training/validation/test proportions of 80/5/15 percent, following the T2M protocol. No subject-disjoint or held-out semantic-combination split is reported for the composition demonstrations.
metrics: FID, top-k R-precision, text-motion multimodal distance, diversity and multimodality use pretrained T2M embeddings. Average inference time per sentence (AITS) and length-dependent timing assess efficiency.

method: MotionCLIP trains a Transformer motion autoencoder whose latent code aligns with frozen CLIP text and rendered-image embeddings. conditions: Text or image embeddings can drive decoding; existing motions provide codes for editing and interpolation. Text labels and rendered frames supervise alignment during training. summary: MLD compresses motions with a VAE before conditional latent diffusion, substantially reducing denoising cost.

method: TRACE separates body, hand, and object motion through aligned temporal VAEs, then couples all latent streams with a joint flow network whose velocity predictions depend on the complete interaction state. Decoded estimates receive contact, object-frame anchoring, and timing supervision; a language branch also supports interaction understanding.

title: PAMI: Part Anchored Motion for Text to Human-Object Interaction Generation
summary: Body-part-relative object votes structure a latent interaction model; coarse generation is followed by contact-oriented surface refinement.
limitations: Single human and single rigid object with known canonical geometry. The bounded refiner cannot repair a wrong action, severe temporal misalignment or large trajectory error; novel-shape generalization remains future work. Contact refinement is not a force-based grasp or continuous collision certificate.
method: Represents object trajectories as learned votes from human body-part anchors plus a free-motion component. A part-factorized VAE preserves human/object coupling; a text- and mesh-conditioned rectified-flow generator samples the latent. A recursive refiner reads long-range body-to-surface and short-range hand surface probes to correct interaction geometry.

evaluation: Table 1 compares HOI generators. Tables 2–3 ablate part-factorization, anchoring/voting and refiner geometry; supplementary experiments evaluate recursion depth. The refiner is also applied without retraining to LIGHT and InterAct-generated outputs.

data_split: Evaluates the standard InterAct benchmark and uses its training partition for normalization. metrics: R-Precision, MM-Dist, FID, diversity, foot-skating ratio, penetration depth, contact ratio and contact precision/recall/F1 for hands and full body. Tables report generation variability/confidence intervals.

title: InterAct: Advancing Large-Scale Versatile 3D Human-Object Interaction Generation
summary: Consolidates HOI sources, refines artifacts and hands, augments under contact invariance, and benchmarks six generation/completion tasks.
limitations: Synthetic augmentation is not new motion capture. Hands are corrected under assumptions suitable for grasp conformity rather than high dexterity. Contact/penetration improvements and text-feature scores do not establish force consistency, independent ancestor-disjoint composition or arbitrary object generalization.
method: Consolidates seven whole-body HOI sources with common surface markers, object BPS geometry and checked human/GPT-4 text annotations. Optimization corrects body/contact artifacts, then hands; augmentation shifts object trajectories and realigns humans while preserving near-contact distances. A transformer diffusion baseline jointly predicts motion and marker-to-object contact vectors, with interaction-aware text features and optional contact guidance. Six tasks distinguish language generation, inpainting, prediction and simulated imitation.
conditions: Task-dependent text/action labels, object shape and trajectories, human motion, past HOI or complete reference interactions. Object-conditioned human generation uses future object motion as an input and is not unconstrained object-trajectory generation.
evaluation: Tables 2–8 separate correction, generation and conditional prediction. Corrected versus raw PhysHOI imitation is demonstrated on four selected sequences over 2,048 environments; this is a narrower experiment than full-corpus executability.
evidence_locator: Sections 3.1–3.3, 4 and 5.1–5.5; Tables 2–8; Supplement C.2–C.7 and E.
data_split: Supplement C: text/action generation partitions each source 9:1 train/test; object-to-human separates 168 training and 29 unseen test objects; human-to-object uses 10:1. Prediction trains on 90 percent and tests on the held-out BEHAVE 10 percent.
metrics: FID, R-precision, MM-Dist, diversity/multimodality; penetration depth/contact ratio; marker error, foot sliding, contact precision/recall/accuracy/F1; object translation/quaternion error; imitation success.

title: InteractMove: Text-Controlled Human-Object Interaction Generation in 3D Scenes with Movable Objects
summary: InterActMove introduces text-conditioned joint human/object generation in scenes with movable objects. AGCA first grounds the referenced object, predicts hand-object affordances, and denoises interaction with local scene features. Contact/penetration losses and test-time penetration guidance encourage target interaction and scene compatibility.
limitations: Grounding mistakes propagate through the pipeline. Learned realism and sampled geometric collision scores are incomplete physical proxies. Exact partition details remain a reporting gap, and scene augmentation must not be counted as independent captured interaction. No force-based certification is established.
method: InterActMove introduces text-conditioned joint human/object generation in scenes with movable objects. AGCA first grounds the referenced object, predicts hand-object affordances, and denoises interaction with local scene features. Contact/penetration losses and test-time penetration guidance encourage target interaction and scene compatibility.
conditions: Free-form text and a 3D scene containing separate object point clouds; a pretrained grounding module selects the target instance. Object geometry, affordance features, and surrounding local geometry condition generated body motion and object trajectories.
evaluation: Tables 2–3 compare interaction generation on the new dataset and TRUMANS subset; ablations remove grounding, affordance, local scene modeling, and collision-aware components. Scene/object augmentation adjusts object placement and interaction trajectories before diffusion-based refinement.
evidence_locator: §3 and Table 1 (dataset/augmentation), §§4.1–4.5 (AGCA), §5.1 metric definitions, Tables 2–4 (comparisons and ablations).
data_split: The constructed dataset contains 618 sequences, 71 objects, 21 scenes, and approximately 2.2 million frames. Evaluation also uses the movable-object subset of TRUMANS. Exact train/test proportions and subject/recording split units are not reported in the inspected main experiment description.
metrics: Goal Distance averages minimum human-object surface distance; Multimodality measures L2 variation for a fixed prompt/scene. Physical Realism is a pretrained frame classifier score, not a dynamics calculation. Non-collision Score measures the proportion of frames without detected penetration.

title: PrimHOI: Compositional Human-Object Interaction via Reusable Primitives
summary: Composes relative-geometry interaction primitives spatially and temporally through hierarchical planning, targeting unseen multi-object tasks.
limitations: Hand-designed primitive vocabulary and small designed task battery bound zero-shot claims. Requires known geometry and reliable symbolic preconditions; primitive planning differs from a unified learned sequence generator. Public repository presence does not establish a released runnable implementation.
method: Factors interactions into relative-geometry primitives such as grasp, clamp and support. Symbolic state transitions compose these primitives, geometric optimization builds key poses, and a retrained contact-guided diffusion controller fills temporal intervals while preserving active constraints.
conditions: Task instruction, known objects and relative contact geometry. LLM/PDDL-HOI planning produces subgoal graphs, then primitive contact factors specify key poses and object paths; LocalControl generates intermediate human motion with contact constraints and post-optimization.
evaluation: Tables 1–3 compare direct GPT planning, primitive hints and PDDL-HOI, then IK/ProgMoGen and LocalControl with/without intermediate trajectories and multiple runs. Authors explicitly avoid relying on distribution FID for out-of-distribution multi-object cases.
evidence_locator: Sections 3.1–3.4, 4.1–4.4; Tables 1–3; Appendix B evaluation details.
data_split: Primitive sources mix OMOMO, BEHAVE and analytic support functions; LocalControl retrains on a No-Walk HumanML3D variant. No conventional held-out-task percentage is reported. Planner tests three designed tasks, with five/five/ten trials, distinct from low-level contact-guidance experiments.
metrics: Planner success rate, action-count efficiency and solution diversity. Motion tests report maximum joint acceleration and constraint errors, plus human-rated success/naturality on 1–10 scales. FID/R-Precision/diversity apply only to matched training-data variants.

title: InterDiff: Generating 3D Human-Object Interactions with Physics-Informed Diffusion
summary: Interaction diffusion forecasts human/object motion and a physics-informed correction predictor refines denoised interactions.
limitations: Intuitive physics is a learned correction, not a dynamics solver. Skeleton-only contacts are ill-defined and omit penetration/contact losses. Best-of-many oracle scores should not be read as single-output accuracy; short forecasting and GRAB visualization do not prove text-conditioned task composition.
method: Predicts future human-object interaction using a transformer diffusion model conditioned on past interaction and object geometry. A correction scheduler identifies likely penetration or loss of contact and chooses a reference frame attached to a human surface marker or the ground. A separate spatial-temporal graph predictor models simpler object dynamics in those coordinates; its prediction is transformed back and blended into denoising. Components train separately.
conditions: Past human/object motion plus object shape. Typical BEHAVE setup gives ten historical frames and predicts 25 future frames, with autoregressive continuation for longer horizons; no text condition is required.
evaluation: Tables compare InterRNN, InterVAE and skeletal prediction baselines. A 100-frame rollout tests long-term prediction; user comparisons assess physical fidelity, while correction/reference ablations probe the inductive bias.
evidence_locator: Sections 3.1–3.2 and 4.1–4.4; Tables 1–4; Figures 3 and 7.
data_split: Uses official BEHAVE train/test partition. On skeleton-based HOI, 18,352 twenty-frame sequences include 582 evaluation sequences with unseen objects; predicts ten future from ten past frames. Cross-dataset experiment trains on BEHAVE and evaluates GRAB without fine-tuning.
metrics: MPJPE-H and MPJPE-O measure global human joints/object keypoints in millimeters; translation error is L2, rotation error uses quaternion difference, and penetration measures object vertices inside the human. Best-of-many evaluation explicitly selects lowest candidate errors.

title: Template Free Reconstruction of Human-object Interaction with Procedural Interaction Generation
summary: Procedurally creates varied human-object interaction pairs and trains an image-conditioned reconstruction model for unseen objects.

HDM does not handle multiple humans/objects, and contact-preserving optimization is not a dynamic interaction certificate.
method: Category-specific autoencoder correspondences transfer contacts to replacement objects; joint pose optimization preserves contact and reduces collisions, followed by textured rendering. HDM reconstructs joint then separate human/object point clouds.
conditions: Procedural generator consumes captured interaction seeds and replacement object shapes with category correspondences. HDM reconstruction consumes an RGB image, then predicts joint and separated human/object point clouds without a known test object template.
evaluation: Section 4 compares HDM with interaction reconstruction baselines, procedural training-data variants and joint/separate denoising designs. Real-image tests include unseen categories; supplementary analyses examine data scaling, diffusion refinement and detailed shape fidelity.
evidence_locator: Sections 3.1–3.3, 4.1–4.4; reconstruction result tables; supplementary Sections B–C (ablation/limitations).

summary: Intent-object text encoding and separate variational autoregressors coordinate arms and body for full-body object interaction.
limitations: Motion is represented by fifteen keyframes at roughly 8–10 fps before interpolation. The setting assumes a reachable object and lacks scene navigation; object optimization does not certify stable contacts, physical forces or successful long locomotion-manipulation sequences.

title: GOAL: Generating 4D Whole-Body Motion for Hand-Object Grasping
summary: GNet predicts a whole-body goal grasp and MNet produces approach motion with coordinated hands, head and body.
limitations: Approach distance is bounded and longer navigation remains future work. The method lacks full surrounding-scene awareness and focuses on grasp acquisition, not subsequent object manipulation or release. Overlapping window counts must not be mistaken for independent captured sequences.
method: Generates a whole-body grasping goal with GNet, a conditional generative model conditioned on object geometry/pose, then uses autoregressive MNet to produce approach motion from the starting body state. Interaction-aware vertex offsets connect body and object geometry; optimization refines both goal grasp and generated motion using predicted Euclidean-space interaction features. MNet generates ten future frames per iteration and rolls forward to the grasp.
conditions: An object mesh, its position/orientation, and a starting human pose/shape roughly 0.5–1.5 meters away. No free-text command or future object trajectory is required.
evaluation: Compares GNet before/after optimization and ground-truth grasps, and studies MNet output horizon. Generated motion has 13.7 percent sliding frames versus 6.7 percent for ground truth under its stated metric.

data_split: Trains on GRAB right-hand stable grasps and approach subsequences. Supplement reports approximately 160K/26K/12.5K static frames and 40K/7K/3K motion windows for train/test/validation. Windows contain ten past, one current and ten future frames; exact source-group holdout membership is not restated.
metrics: Static goals and generated motions receive five-point perceptual ratings for body realism, foot-ground contact, grasp and head orientation. MNet horizon ablations report body/hand/foot vertex distances and pose/translation reconstruction errors. Foot sliding counts frames whose selected ground-near vertex moves over one centimeter.

title: SAGA: Stochastic Whole-Body Grasping with Contact
summary: SAGA combines WholeGrasp-VAE, which samples full-body grasp poses and contacts around an object, with MotionFill-VAE, which fills a transition from an initial body state to the sampled grasp. Marker-based optimization then fits SMPL-X and improves contact and collision behavior.
limitations: Optimization and contact thresholds add sensitivity and runtime. End-grasp quality does not guarantee every intermediate frame is collision-free or dynamically feasible; a stationary target and short approach window limit long manipulation claims. GRAB-derived grouping must preserve object and source ancestry.
method: SAGA combines WholeGrasp-VAE, which samples full-body grasp poses and contacts around an object, with MotionFill-VAE, which fills a transition from an initial body state to the sampled grasp. Marker-based optimization then fits SMPL-X and improves contact and collision behavior.
conditions: A target object mesh and starting human state; the method samples an ending whole-body grasp and the intervening motion. It does not require an entire future object path, but its primary interaction is approaching and grasping a stationary target rather than unrestricted long manipulation.
evaluation: Tables 1–2 evaluate grasp sampling and optimization losses; motion experiments compare transition models and local/global completion components. Qualitative HO3D results assess unseen object geometries. Explicitly distinguish best-of-ten reference matching from a single deployed sample.
evidence_locator: §3 (WholeGrasp/MotionFill and optimizers), §4 experiments and Tables 1–2; supplementary training-data section naming 41/4/6 objects and motion metrics.

MotionFill uses 62-frame approach-to-grasp clips at 30 fps; AMASS supplies 61-frame pretraining clips. HO3D objects test additional shape transfer without a stated statistical split ratio.
metrics: Contact Ratio measures proximity contact; interpenetration volume/depth quantify mesh intersections; APD measures diversity. Marker ADE compares deterministic predictions, with minimum error over 10 samples for stochastic motion. PSKL-J compares acceleration power spectra as a smoothness proxy.

title: InteractAgent: Agentic Human Motion Interaction with Memory-Augmented Reflection
summary: Wraps a frozen motion executor with local visual recovery and cross-attempt planning reflection.
method: The same multimodal LLM performs scene analysis, planning, visual evaluation and reflection. A frozen Motion-Agent MotionLLM realizes action lists. Online observation chooses continue/redo/replan; inference-time memory informs later attempts without weight updates.

metrics: Execution/task success is reported by complexity. Physical validity uses body-scene SDF penetration, including maximum and highest-10%-frame mean, preventing long noninteractive intervals from diluting severe collisions.
evaluation: Tables 1–3 compare training-free variants, a supervised UniHSI-CoCo baseline, planner backbones and executors. Ablations separate online feedback from offline/memory reflection.
limitations: The planner and visual evaluator share a backbone, so reported success is not an independent physical certificate. Occlusion, view sampling, executor limits and retry cost remain; geometric penetration must be reported separately.

title: World2HOSI: A Multi-Expert Harness for Long-Horizon Human-Object-Scene Interaction Generation
summary: Orchestrates navigation, object and scene interaction experts around persistent scene state, reconciling boundaries and updating object effects.
limitations: Expert availability and planning assumptions bound transfer. Bounded residual control cannot rescue fundamentally infeasible references; a multi-expert harness is not one unified text-to-motion model or a cross-dataset dataset-construction method.

title: Scaling Up Dynamic Human-Scene Interaction Modeling
summary: TRUMANS captures human and part-level dynamic-object interaction across indoor scene configurations; autoregressive diffusion supports extended motion synthesis.
limitations: Augmentation and scene generalization differ from unseen action-chain or actor generalization. Geometric penetration and foot-contact measurements do not establish dynamics. Action timing/progress is supplied, limiting autonomous high-level planning claims.
method: Captures whole-body human motion and tracked dynamic objects in reconstructed scenes, then augments human/object appearance and geometry while preserving interaction alignment. An autoregressive diffusion generator rolls out short episodes using local scene context and frame-level action labels; an action-progress indicator maintains continuity across episode boundaries.
conditions: Current/historical body state, local scene occupancy, action labels and progress; dynamic-object context is included for interaction. This is action-controlled scene generation, not free-form text planning.
evaluation: Compares static HSI against scene-generation baselines and dynamic interaction against GRAB-trained IMoS/GOAL. Each trajectory receives five generated variants. Ablations remove data augmentation or the progress indicator; human ratings assess resemblance to captured motion.
evidence_locator: Sections 3.1–3.3, 4.1–4.4; Sections 5.1–5.4, Tables 2–5; Appendix A.4.
data_split: Dataset records seven participants across 100 scene configurations for over fifteen hours. Evaluation includes ten unseen indoor scenes from PROX, Replica, ScanNet and ScanNet++; precise training/test proportions within TRUMANS are not stated in the inspected main protocol.
metrics: Static HSI: contact rate and mean/maximum penetration. Dynamic object-level interaction: FID, diversity, scene penetration and MoCap-discrimination success (Table 3). Downstream mesh/contact tasks report MPVE/MPJPE/PA-MPJPE and contact precision/recall/F1/geodesic error.

title: CIRCLE: Capture In Rich Contextual Environments
summary: Captures real human movement in perceived virtual scenes and learns scene-conditioned full-body reaching.
limitations: The authors note persistent collisions and foot sliding. A nearly static baseline can misleadingly score well on sliding. VR capture does not provide physical contact reactions, and task-held-out reaching does not imply unseen scenes, dexterous grasping or object dynamics.
method: Captures full-body reaching while participants view virtual environments through a VR headset. Real capture space remains empty, while the simulator supplies exact scene geometry and rendered observations. A scene-aware transformer refines an initialized motion between a start pose and target wrist location, using local body/scene features from BPS or pretrained PointNet++ encodings. Training combines root, joint position, rotation and forward-kinematics losses.
conditions: Initial body pose, scene geometry and a target right-hand/wrist position; this is contextual reaching, not dynamic object manipulation. Virtual scene contact has no corresponding physical object force feedback.
evaluation: Tables 2–3 compare scene-conditioned variants, a no-scene baseline and GOAL modified to receive a ground-truth goal pose. All use the same data; task-held-out results degrade, and scene features improve reaching/collision behavior.
evidence_locator: Sections 3, 4, 5.1–5.3 and 6; Tables 2–3; Figure 6.
data_split: 3,018 reaching sequences: random split has 2,565 train/453 test; task split has 2,578 train/440 test, holding out start/goal region pairs (109 training and 19 test tasks). Five subjects perform about ten hours across nine scenes.
metrics: Success means final wrist within ten centimeters of target. Also measures distance to goal, cumulative scene collision depth, foot sliding, mean vertex/joint-position errors, root translation and joint-orientation discrepancy.

Scene/object point-cloud features condition denoising; gradients of collision, contact, or task costs steer samples at inference. method: SceneDiffuser unifies conditional diffusion, differentiable objective guidance, and planning. Scene/object point-cloud features condition denoising; gradients of collision, contact, or task costs steer samples at inference. The framework handles poses, motions, dexterous grasps, path planning, and robot motion planning with task-specific representations.
conditions: 3D scene or object point clouds, optional start pose, and differentiable goals or constraints. The generated variable changes by task, so dexterous grasp and robot planning findings should not be merged into a single full-body language-conditioned manipulation claim.

title: Revisit Human-Scene Interaction via Space Occupancy
summary: Uses space occupancy to connect locomotion and interaction control; evaluates reaching and extended indoor action sequences.
limitations: Occupancy supervision assesses geometric compatibility, not force balance. Dynamic-scene and trajectory-conditioned object experiments are present, but shared-object OMOMO evaluation and qualitative door examples do not establish unseen-object or unrestricted task-chain generalization.
method: Constructs a Motion Occupancy Base from motion-only data by representing surrounding feasible occupied/free space, turning captured motion into synthetic interaction supervision. A lightweight autoregressive transformer controller predicts future state using historical pose and optional controls. Occupancy-field and penetration losses discourage collisions, and online control guides endpoints or paths.

evaluation: Main MOB/CIRCLE tests evaluate reaching and collision avoidance with held-out sequences. Appendix C.2 fine-tunes on OMOMO contact trajectories; C.3 demonstrates a rotating door and sudden occupancy changes. These are distinct protocols, not one uniform benchmark.

The OMOMO fine-tuning extension shares all 15 object identities across train/test and reports one evaluation run.
metrics: Goal-reaching success, distance to goal, cumulative collision depth and foot sliding. Scene/occupancy interaction evaluations compare feasibility and target accuracy rather than language retrieval. The OMOMO extension also reports root translation/rotation error, Hand JPE and MPJPE.

title: Compositional Human-Scene Interaction Synthesis with Semantic Control
summary: COINS encodes body surface points and objects in a joint latent space, permitting multiple atomic action-object pairs without corresponding composite training examples.

PelvisVAE samples global pelvis placement; BodyVAE generates local body vertices and contact, followed by optimization. metrics: Semantic contact compares action-weighted contact to a threshold from training data. Non-collision is the fraction of vertices with nonnegative scene SDF. Diversity uses 50-cluster entropy and distance to centers; user studies assess naturalness and semantic agreement.

title: PiGraphs: Learning Interaction Snapshots from Observations
summary: Probabilistic prototype interaction graphs couple body poses, object geometry, contact and visual attention for scene and pose synthesis.
limitations: Explicitly restricted to static scenes without interaction dynamics or ordering. Sampling can get trapped by poor initial placements; commodity depth resolution limits small objects. Novel static relations do not establish continuous locomotion-manipulation composition.
method: Learns prototypical interaction graphs from RGB-D observations aligned with reconstructed scenes. Nodes represent body joints and object geometry; contact and gaze edges store spatial feature distributions. Sampling poses and arranging retrieved objects maximize learned interaction likelihoods. Aggregating action priors supports new verb-noun combinations and multiple simultaneous static relations.

title: Learning Generalizable Human Motion Generator with Reinforcement Learning
summary: Uses reinforcement learning and contrastive text-motion rewards on paired data and synthetic text-only prompts to improve generalization.
limitations: Reward models themselves are trained on limited paired data and prioritize coarse semantic alignment over fine motion. Optimizing learned alignment can exploit evaluator biases. Synthetic prompt generalization does not by itself establish unseen physical skills, object-state consistency, or independent contact-quality improvement.

Rewards use pretrained contrastive text/motion encoders: generated-motion distance to text, and optionally to paired ground-truth motion. summary: Multi-view RGB-D body-object interaction data with body/object fits and contacts across everyday objects and locations.
limitations: Known object geometry, RGB-D acquisition and fitted supervision constrain applicability. Occlusion and noisy point clouds remain relevant; contact annotations are not measured force or friction labels. The method jointly registers SMPL and a prescanned rigid object to multi-view depth observations. Neural predictions provide human-surface correspondence, object orientation and explicit contact correspondences, which enter optimization to align body/object meshes rather than fitting them independently. The released fits are pseudo-ground truth from this capture/optimization pipeline.
conditions: Multi-view RGB-D, human/object segmentation and known rigid object mesh; tracking estimates human pose/shape, object pose and contact. This is observation-conditioned reconstruction, not text-driven motion generation.
evaluation: Compares PHOSA adapted to its input setup, IPNet and LoopReg, then tests learned object orientation and contact fitting. The authors note that contact removal can produce conspicuous floating despite small differences in aggregate vertex error.

metrics: Human SMPL vertex-to-vertex error and object vertex-to-vertex error are reported in centimeters. Qualitative contact plausibility supplements geometric error; tables ablate orientation and contact terms and compare body registration.

summary: Introduces HumanML3D and a stochastic text-to-motion baseline.

method: Samples duration from text, then generates motion snippets with a temporal VAE.
conditions: Natural-language description and sampled output duration. A text-conditioned temporal VAE predicts short movement snippet codes, whose decoder reconstructs continuous joint motion; curriculum training progressively lengthens predicted sequences.

The dataset expands semantic coverage and provides a common evaluation representation; its real-motion statistics are reference values, not model successes. title: InterCap: Joint Markerless 3D Tracking of Humans and Objects in Interaction
summary: InterCap estimates jointly moving SMPL-X humans and rigid objects from synchronized multiview RGB-D observations. Segmentation, detected joints, object pose initialization, and temporally coupled optimization combine depth fitting, pose priors, contact encouragement, and collision constraints to reconstruct captured interactions without optical body markers.

Markerless capture improves accessibility but cannot establish exact dense contact or any text-conditioned compositional generation capability.
method: InterCap estimates jointly moving SMPL-X humans and rigid objects from synchronized multiview RGB-D observations. Segmentation, detected joints, object pose initialization, and temporally coupled optimization combine depth fitting, pose priors, contact encouragement, and collision constraints to reconstruct captured interactions without optical body markers.
conditions: Multiple calibrated RGB-D streams and known scanned object geometry. The method reconstructs observed interaction rather than generating new motion from text. Fitted body/object trajectories and proximity-derived contact are dataset outputs with their own reconstruction uncertainty.
evaluation: Section 5 analyzes contact heatmaps, reconstruction errors, object/human alignment, and mesh penetration. Real data average vertex-to-cloud errors are 20.29 mm for bodies and 18.50 mm for objects; these are sensor-fit distances, not independent full-surface ground-truth errors.

metrics: Body/object vertex-to-segmented-point-cloud distances quantify observation fit. Mean penetration depth characterizes reconstructed contact frames; contact maps threshold closest human-object distances at 4.5 mm. Per-frame comparisons with the segmented depth observations assess fitting accuracy, separately from qualitative render inspection; no independent full-body ground-truth trajectory is assumed.

title: MaskAdapt: Learning Flexible Motion Adaptation via Mask-Invariant Prior for Physics-Based Characters
summary: MaskAdapt learns an adversarial base policy with observation masks and a mask-invariant regularizer, then trains a residual adaptation policy controlling selected parts. The base preserves non-adapted behavior while residual rewards teach new local motions or tracking, allowing dynamic changes of the controlled body region.
limitations: Conflicting commands on mechanically coupled parts can fail, such as different leg tasks. Partial tracking inherits the kinematic generator’s semantic errors. Evaluation in a particular simulator and selected reference combinations does not establish robust manipulation or real-hardware transfer.
method: MaskAdapt learns an adversarial base policy with observation masks and a mask-invariant regularizer, then trains a residual adaptation policy controlling selected parts. The base preserves non-adapted behavior while residual rewards teach new local motions or tracking, allowing dynamic changes of the controlled body region.
conditions: Proprioception, body-part masks, and task/reference signals; text-driven examples rely on a pretrained kinematic generator supplying partial trajectories. The simulated character has 22 bodies and 63 degrees of freedom, so this is embodied policy adaptation rather than unrestricted body-motion decoding.

metrics: R-Precision, FID, multimodal distance and diversity; bone-based penetration, floating and sliding, with five-millimeter ground tolerance. Environment experiments evaluate adaptation/tracking and compare inference speed.

title: CLoSD: Closing the Loop between Simulation and Diffusion for multi-task character control
summary: Closes a feedback loop between an autoregressive text/target-conditioned diffusion planner and an RL tracker for task sequences.
limitations: Demonstrated state-machine task sequences do not establish arbitrary task generalization or dexterous manipulation. A single lightweight tracker omits PHC’s full recovery machinery. Simulation success and selected-joint targets do not establish force-accurate human data or real-robot transfer.
method: Combines DiP, an autoregressive text/target-conditioned diffusion planner, with a universal PHC-style physics tracker. The tracker executes planned frames, then its actual simulated motion supplies the next planner prefix. Closed-loop PPO fine-tuning keeps the planner fixed and adapts the tracker across tasks. A high-level state machine switches text and target conditions when explicit task-success events occur; it is not learned open-ended task planning.
conditions: Text plus the target location of a selected body joint; actual executed motion history closes the loop. Tasks include locomotion goal reaching, striking, sitting and getting up.
evaluation: Tables compare task-specific and multitask agents, open-loop execution, no fine-tuning and altered replanning lengths. Physics improves skating while feature-distribution scores can degrade relative to the unconstrained DiP planner.
evidence_locator: Sections 4.1–4.4, 5.1–5.3 and 6; Tables 1–3; task success definitions and physics metric paragraph.
data_split: DiP trains on HumanML3D and the tracker on AMASS. Text generation follows HumanML3D benchmark evaluation without a new declared proportional split. Task success uses 1,000 episodes per task with randomized placements; these are environment trials, not held-out motion-recording identities.
metrics: Task-specific success rates; FID, R-precision, MM-Dist and diversity; physical proxies measure ground penetration, floating and skating. Runtime, generation FPS and plan-length/diffusion-step ablations assess efficiency.
