title: Learning Multi-Modal Whole-Body Control for Real-World Humanoid Robots
summary: Masked Humanoid Controller learns one policy to track selectively masked motion directives while obeying locomotion commands. A staged curriculum, offset-aware future directives, motion/style rewards, perturbations, and dynamics randomization teach compatibility between whole-body mimicry, upper-body motion, standing, and joystick walking.
limitations: The chosen motion corpus avoids the most aggressive behaviors and robot morphology restricts transfer. Inconsistent directives and limited mask patterns remain open issues. Real-world task demonstrations do not establish text-semantic composition or arbitrary object interaction.
method: Masked Humanoid Controller learns one policy to track selectively masked motion directives while obeying locomotion commands. A staged curriculum, offset-aware future directives, motion/style rewards, perturbations, and dynamics randomization teach compatibility between whole-body mimicry, upper-body motion, standing, and joystick walking.
conditions: Motion target trajectories with body-part masks, root velocity/turn commands, standing indicator, and robot proprioception. Outputs are joint PD setpoints for Digit. The policy combines control modalities; a natural-language generator is not part of the principal system.
evaluation: Tables 2–5 compare walking/standing, offset-aware baselines, dataset scaling, and curriculum ablations. Full/partial mimicry follows each directive once, while locomotion episodes last ten seconds. Real Digit tests evaluate the 20 setA motions and demonstrate upper-body tracking with locomotion.
evidence_locator: Method sections Motion Directives/Curriculum/Reward Design; Motion Directive Dataset (20/20/35), Experimental Setup and Metrics, Tables 2–5; Real-World Experiments and conclusion.
data_split: Uses 75 retargeted trajectories partitioned into setA (20), setB (20), and setC (35), with increasing difficulty and mixed AMASS/animation/optimized/video sources. Models trained on A, AB, and ABC are evaluated across sets; this is not a random percentage subject split.
metrics: Mean End-Effector Position Error (EMEPE) measures specified limb positions relative to the torso; root drift measures global locomotion/standing error; failure percentage measures terminated episodes. Perturbation tests apply 50N/100N torso forces; hardware tests omit root error when global localization is unavailable.

title: MaskedMimic: Unified Physics-Based Character Control Through Masked Motion Inpainting
summary: Unifies masked keyframes, objects, text and mixed descriptions as partial motion constraints for simulated character control.
limitations: Goal engineering still specifies task sequences. Simulator success and sparse-target agreement do not certify arbitrary language-task composition, manipulable-object dynamics or real-robot transfer; performance depends on filtered reference coverage and teacher quality.
method: First trains a fully constrained physics tracker, then distills it into a partially constrained controller through conditional variational motion inpainting. Randomly masked targets teach a learned prior to infer missing motion. One unified controller consumes heterogeneous goal tokens and combines sparse keyframes, language, objects and terrain without task-specific fine-tuning.
conditions: Proprioception, optional partial joint targets, text embeddings, object bounding boxes and terrain; missing conditions are masked. Simple finite-state goal programs switch constraints to create longer behaviors.
evaluation: Tables compare full-body/VR tracking, irregular terrain, path following and object interactions. Evaluations use the prior mean for precision, while latent sampling explores diversity. The same model handles all tested tasks, and finite-state constraints enable sequential demonstrations.
evidence_locator: Sections 5–6.5, Sections 7.1–7.3; Tables 1–6; goal-program description in task evaluation.
data_split: Filtered AMASS supplies motion, HumanML3D supplies language and object-interaction data supplies sitting conditions. Evaluates AMASS training/test partitions and held-out sitting objects. Exact aggregate partition proportions are not reported; held-out objects are distinct from held-out motion categories.
metrics: Success rate, global MPJPE, observed-joint MPOJPE, path/orientation error and task-specific target errors. Full tracking fails if average joint deviation exceeds 0.5 meters in any frame.

title: DiffMimic: Efficient Motion Mimicking with Differentiable Physics
summary: Uses differentiable physics for efficient reference motion imitation.
limitations: Differentiable contact can produce noisy gradients and local minima, and the simulator relaxes joint limits for smoother optimization. Replaying demonstration states is a training intervention, not demonstrated autonomous recovery. Efficient reference imitation does not establish unseen motion composition, language grounding or object-interaction planning.
method: Optimizes a motion-imitation policy through differentiable Brax physics using analytical gradients propagated along simulated trajectories. The policy produces proportional-derivative joint targets from local body state and a reference phase. Demonstration replay replaces simulated states with corresponding reference states when deviation exceeds a threshold, helping avoid poor local minima and unstable long-horizon gradients. No learned world-model approximation is required.
conditions: A reference motion clip and its phase, simulated humanoid state, and known physics configuration. This is clip-conditioned control/learning, not semantic composition or text-conditioned synthesis.
evaluation: Compares DeepMimic, Spacetime Bound and AMP. Ablations compare full-horizon differentiation, short truncation, random demonstration replacement and threshold replay; per-frame errors expose behavior hidden by average imitation scores.
evidence_locator: Sections 3.1–3.3, 4.1–4.4 and 5; Figures 2–4 and 6–8; Equation 4.1.
data_split: Per-motion imitation setup has no dataset-level train/test recording split. Reference clips are inherited from AMP’s mixture of mocap and authored animation. Cyclic-motion policies train with four-second rollouts and are evaluated for 20-second continuation.
metrics: Average root-relative Euclidean joint pose error in meters, aligned by dynamic time warping; sample count and wall time measure training efficiency. Evaluation includes completing 20-second cyclic rollouts without falling.

title: Perpetual Humanoid Control for Real-time Simulated Avatars
summary: Scales physics-based imitation with recovery from falls and noisy reference motion.
limitations: Consumes privileged future references; success is tracking rather than autonomous generation or task planning. Progressive training is costly, and scene/terrain awareness remains limited. Excluding object interaction prevents interpreting reported rates as human-object contact or loco-manipulation execution accuracy.
method: Progressive multiplicative control allocates capacity for difficult motions and recovery.
conditions: Full future reference motion and simulated humanoid state for imitation; recovery observations handle falls and imperfect upstream pose estimates. Progressive multiplicative control adds capacity for difficult motions without residual external forces.
evaluation: Table 1 compares UHC with/without residual forces on captured trajectories. Further tests assess recovery, noisy poses and real-time upstream reconstruction. Ablations examine primitive capacity and recovery training, showing physics-based imitation as an infrastructure component. Recovery transitions are trained deliberately rather than inferred from imitation success alone.
evidence_locator: Sections 3.1–3.3, 4.1–4.4; Table 1 and recovery/noisy-input result tables; limitations.
data_split: High-quality tests contain 11,313 AMASS training, 140 AMASS test and 140 Human3.6M motion sequences after excluding human-object interactions. Additional noisy/image-derived inputs test robustness. These are motion imitation partitions, not a language or compositional action split.
metrics: Imitation success, global/local MPJPE, acceleration/velocity error and recovery behavior. Tables distinguish controllers with residual force control from PHC without it; results average three runs.

title: Universal Humanoid Motion Representations for Physics-Based Control
summary: PULSE first trains a stronger PHC+ motion imitator, then distills its motor knowledge into a variational bottleneck with a proprioception-conditioned latent prior. A frozen decoder maps latent actions into motor controls, while new high-level RL policies learn downstream tasks in that reusable action space.
limitations: Simulator rewards and cleaned reference coverage influence results. Reusing a latent action space still requires task-policy training and does not imply arbitrary semantic combinations. Controller tracking is insufficient to assess detailed object grasping, tactile realism, or real humanoid deployment.
method: PULSE first trains a stronger PHC+ motion imitator, then distills its motor knowledge into a variational bottleneck with a proprioception-conditioned latent prior. A frozen decoder maps latent actions into motor controls, while new high-level RL policies learn downstream tasks in that reusable action space.
conditions: Robot/humanoid proprioception and task goals, including reference poses, VR controller positions, target speed, reaching/striking, or terrain context. A task-specific high-level policy is trained for each downstream problem; this is not zero-shot natural-language skill composition.
evaluation: Table 1 compares PHC/PHC+/PULSE imitation; Table 2 compares VR tracking against ASE/CALM variants; task learning curves test reach, speed, strike, and terrain. Representation/prior ablations examine coverage and control benefits, while failure recovery is part of the imitator.
evidence_locator: §§4.1–4.3 (PHC+, variational distillation, downstream RL), §5 metrics/experiments, Tables 1–2; appendix B.1 (cleaning/counts), B.2 (control).
data_split: Cleaned AMASS contains 11,313 training and 138 test sequences after removing unsuitable artifacts. The split is explicitly sequence-based in reported counts; real VR data add 14 trajectories. Downstream RL tasks use simulator goal distributions rather than a common held-out text-motion partition.
metrics: Success requires average per-joint tracking distance below 0.5m throughout the reference. Global/root-relative MPJPE, velocity error, and acceleration error measure imitation; VR uses three-controller tracking error when full-body truth is unavailable. Normalized undiscounted return evaluates generative downstream tasks.

title: ASE: Large-Scale Reusable Adversarial Skill Embeddings for Physically Simulated Characters
summary: Learns reusable latent motor skills from unsegmented motion using adversarial imitation and unsupervised RL.
limitations: Learned latent availability is bounded by the motion corpus and simulated embodiment. Reward-driven composition is distinct from unseen language combinations or dataset composition. Attached sword/shield geometry does not establish dexterous grasping or general object manipulation.
method: Pretrains a latent-conditioned simulated humanoid with adversarial imitation of unsegmented motion transitions and a mutual-information skill-discovery objective. A discriminator rewards mocap-like movement while an encoder encourages distinguishable latent skills. Downstream high-level RL selects latent codes, reusing the low-level policy and discriminator motion prior.
conditions: Low-level proprioception and a continuous latent skill. Downstream tasks add goal locations, speed, heading or target-object state and hand-designed task rewards; no text-compositional interface is learned.
evaluation: Sections 9–10 test reaching with a sword tip, controlling travel speed/direction, moving to a location and striking a target. Baselines include policies trained from scratch and other skill-prior approaches; demonstrations show natural transitions among reusable skills.
evidence_locator: Sections 5.1–5.5, 7.1–7.2; Sections 9–10; Figures 6–10 and task learning curves.
data_split: Pretraining uses 187 unsegmented clips totaling approximately thirty minutes, including locomotion and sword/shield behaviors. There is no conventional held-out mocap train/test percentage: downstream control tasks evaluate reuse of the pretrained skill space rather than reconstruction of withheld clips.
metrics: Task returns and learning curves, reach/location/speed/steering errors through corresponding reward objectives, strike performance, qualitative skill diversity and imitation quality. Ablations compare latent/objective and motion-prior designs.

title: PhysDiff: Physics-Guided Human Motion Diffusion Model
summary: Interleaves motion diffusion with a simulator-based imitation projection instead of applying physics only after generation.
method: A PPO-trained motion imitation policy tracks selected denoised estimates in IsaacGym. The projected simulated motion conditions subsequent diffusion steps; projection scheduling favors later, lower-noise stages.
conditions: Text or an action label and motion duration, together with a pretrained denoiser and imitation controller. SMPL body attributes condition tracking; PD targets and residual forces support imitation.
data_split: Text-to-motion uses HumanML3D. Action-to-motion uses HumanAct12 and UESTC sequences provided by the cited ACTOR protocol. The checked sections do not establish an independent semantic-combination or object-interaction split.
metrics: FID and text R-precision or action-classification accuracy assess generation. Penetrate and Float measure mesh-ground distances with 5 mm tolerance; Skate measures contacting-foot displacement. Phys-Err sums these distance quantities.
evaluation: Compares MDM/MotionDiffuse backbones, number and timing of projections, and postprocessing-only alternatives. Late-step projection is evaluated separately from simply increasing simulator calls.
limitations: Projection is expensive and depends on controller coverage. Residual-force-assisted simulation and ground-artifact metrics do not establish unassisted physical feasibility, object-contact correctness or hardware execution.
evidence_locator: §§3.1–3.2; §4.1–4.4 and Tables 1–4; Appendices A–C.

title: AMP: Adversarial Motion Priors for Stylized Physics-Based Character Control
summary: Learns motion-style rewards from unstructured clips alongside task rewards; reports emergent skill composition.
limitations: Task-specific policy/discriminator data induce dependencies that complicate transferring priors to new tasks. Discussion focuses mainly on temporal composition and identifies spatial composition as future work. Emergent behavior is simulation/task-reward evidence, not held-out free-text skill-pair generation or measured human interaction data.
method: Learns a discriminator-based motion-style reward from transitions in an unstructured reference-motion collection and combines it with a task reward in goal-conditioned reinforcement learning. Least-squares adversarial training, gradient penalty and a replay buffer stabilize imitation. Policies output joint PD targets; they need not synchronize to or select a specific reference clip. Task-directed temporal skill selection emerges from optimizing task and style together.
conditions: Character state, a task goal and an example motion dataset defining style. The high-level task reward is engineered; language is not the input condition.
evaluation: Demonstrates humanoid, dog and T-Rex control. Importantly, the strike prior contains walking-only and punching-only clips: the policy learns walk-then-punch without a combined demonstration. Compares tracking-based imitation and ablates discriminator gradient penalty/velocity features.
evidence_locator: Sections 5–8.5 and 9; Tables 1–3; Figure 9; Appendix task rewards.
data_split: Uses task-specific motion collections and per-task policy learning, not a recording-level held-out train/test composition split. Single-clip imitation compares three independent training seeds, 32 episodes per model and maximum 20-second episodes.
metrics: Normalized task returns measure task fulfillment; DTW-aligned root-relative pose error in meters measures single-clip imitation. Learning curves and sample counts evaluate efficiency/stability; qualitative sequences illustrate style and transitions.

title: DeepMimic: Example-Guided Deep Reinforcement Learning of Physics-Based Character Skills
summary: DeepMimic trains physics-based policies with PPO to maximize imitation and task rewards. Pose, joint velocity, end-effector, and center-of-mass terms reproduce reference clips; reference-state initialization and early termination improve difficult-skill learning. Multi-clip objectives and policy composition enable broader behavioral repertoires.
limitations: Learned skills depend on reference coverage, simulator fidelity, and reward design; multi-clip capabilities do not prove unseen linguistic task combinations. Simulated Atlas morphology is not hardware deployment. Contact emerging in simulation should not be generalized to dexterous human-object manipulation.
method: DeepMimic trains physics-based policies with PPO to maximize imitation and task rewards. Pose, joint velocity, end-effector, and center-of-mass terms reproduce reference clips; reference-state initialization and early termination improve difficult-skill learning. Multi-clip objectives and policy composition enable broader behavioral repertoires.
conditions: Proprioception, reference phase, and optional task goals or terrain observations. Policies output PD targets for articulated simulated characters, including humanoid, Atlas, T-Rex, and dragon. Explicit reference skills and rewards supply the behavior specification rather than free-form text.
evaluation: Section 6/Table 2 evaluate acrobatic and locomotion skills across characters, while subsequent experiments add task adaptation, perturbation recovery, multi-skill agents, and obstacle traversal. Ablations assess reference initialization and termination; qualitative videos support motion-quality judgments.
evidence_locator: §4 rewards/training, §5 environments/characters, §6 and Table 2 (normalized returns and samples), task adaptation, robustness, multi-skill and ablation subsections.
data_split: Not applicable as a conventional supervised train/test dataset split. Policies learn designated reference clips and are evaluated on simulator episodes, task goals, perturbations, and terrain. Table 2 lists skill-specific training samples and performance rather than held-out human/recording proportions.
metrics: Normalized episode return measures achievement of imitation/task rewards relative to possible reward bounds. Training-sample counts and learning curves measure efficiency; task trials assess recovery, terrain traversal, target accuracy, and skill composition. title: GRAIL: Generating Humanoid Loco-Manipulation from World Models
summary: Grounds generated videos in known 3D scenes/assets, recovers HOI, retargets and trains trackers and visual policies.
limitations: Assumes known 3D assets and simulator-ready scenes. Occlusion, fast motion and inconsistent generated appearance degrade reconstruction; failures are filtered. New motion families can require tracker retraining. Synthetic data and small task-specific real deployment do not establish arbitrary general task-chain composition.
method: Uses asset-conditioned video generation in a known scene, recovers aligned human-object motion, retargets it and trains a task-general humanoid tracker. An object-aware adapter augments a pretrained whole-body controller; visual policies are subsequently distilled for egocentric execution. Synthetic data generation and robot deployment are separate pipeline stages.
conditions: Text/task instructions, known object assets, scene configurations and initial states; tracking uses reference trajectories and privileged simulated state during training. Final visual policies use onboard observations.
evaluation: Section 4 separates generated HOI, loco-manipulation tracking and sim-to-real pick-up/stairs. Baseline and adapter ablations test components. Table 3 reports 84% seen-object and 80% unseen-object pick-up success in the stated small trial set.
evidence_locator: Sections 3.1–3.4; Sections 4.1–4.3, Tables 1–3; Appendix C evaluation settings. Section 6 (Limitations).
data_split: HOI comparison uses twenty ComAsset objects. Synthetic G1 data exceeds 20,000 sequences from 1,000 object assets paired with 1,000 procedurally generated terrain configurations; tracking comparison evaluates 124 motions across 43 objects. Real pick-up separates five seen and five unseen objects, ten trials per object. A single global split ratio is not reported.
metrics: Contact distance, penetration ratio, VLM interaction rating, human/object acceleration smoothness, InterMimic tracking deviations and frame-wise success; G1 tracking SR/object position/local MPJPE; real task success.

title: InterMimicGen: Scaling Humanoid Loco-Manipulation through Self-Evolving Motion Imitation
summary: Retargets heterogeneous HOI, learns a generalist simulation tracker and iteratively retains task-preserving perturbations that execute successfully.
limitations: Validated augmentation densifies existing semantics and may favor easier objects or compound reference errors. Contact preservation treats penetration as zero distance and is not independent grasp-force certification. Real-world examples must not be described as direct transfer of one identical generalist policy across all embodiments.
method: Retargets heterogeneous human-object recordings using interaction meshes, finger-opposition constraints and contact-preserving cleanup. A generalist PPO tracker executes whole-body/object references. Self-evolution edits object placement or body posture while preserving interaction type, intended contacts, object and outcome; each round fine-tunes the tracker, executes candidates and retains successful rollouts. Accepted descendants seed further rounds rather than introducing new task semantics.
conditions: Reference body/object motion, robot morphology and explicit interaction geometry/contact intent. Outputs retargeted references and executable simulated rollouts; text-to-motion is not the learning objective.
evaluation: Compares dexterous retargeters and per-object specialists against one generalist. Hardware paths differ: G1 uses SONIC with finger replay; Booster uses its deployment stack; Vega uses direct retargeted trajectories and slower playback.
evidence_locator: Sections 3.2–3.4 and 4.1–4.5; Tables 1–3; Appendices A, C.2, E.2–E.4, G and H.
data_split: Collection combines 9,030 InterAct and 7,029 HiPHI sequences. Tracking benchmark groups 15 objects into bimanual, sitting and grasping; evaluates trained reference execution, not a declared held-out-recording percentage. Five augmentation rounds use verified seed descendants.
metrics: Hand-contact preservation, slip, penetration, foot sliding, MPJPE, end-effector error, joint acceleration/limits; tracking success means full reference completion without failure thresholds. Reports body/object errors on successes, augmentation growth and before/after tracking success.

title: Weave: Learning Whole-Body Dexterous Loco-Manipulation from Human-Object Interactions
summary: Contact-aware retargeting and approach completion feed a geometry/contact-aware whole-body and finger controller; releases simulated robot-object rollouts.
limitations: Released simulator rollouts are not hardware recordings. Unseen sequence results use familiar objects and harder generated approach prefixes; they do not demonstrate arbitrary new geometry/tasks. Contact-aware tracking is distinct from generating novel human task sequences.
method: Constructs executable interaction references, then tracks them with coordinated body and finger control.
conditions: Retargeted human-object references, geometry/contact descriptors and simulated robot/object state. Approach completion adds locomotion prefixes before manipulation; coordinated body/finger control tracks expected contacts with local reference information.
evaluation: Compares object specialists and a unified multi-object policy; evaluates train performance, transfer to unseen sequences and an oracle trained directly on test references. Failure/termination checks include positional deviation and lost expected contact for ten control steps. The oracle isolates reference-trackability from generalization of the trained controller.
evidence_locator: Sections III–IV (reference/control), Section V.A–V.C; Figures 3–5; evaluation metrics and train/test/oracle protocol.
data_split: Nine-object G1 reference data divide into 7,869 training trajectories (19.56 h) and 1,605 test trajectories (3.67 h). Test sequences use the same objects, with three approach variants per training interaction and five per test interaction, introducing a stated distribution shift.
metrics: Clip-balanced tracking errors, completion success and progress; root/body/finger/object position-orientation measures and contact-related termination. Pooled rates weighted by trajectory count are distinguished from equal-object averages.

title: BeyondMimic: From Motion Tracking to Versatile Humanoid Control via Guided Diffusion
summary: BeyondMimic trains robust whole-body tracking policies with adaptive motion sampling and sim-to-real randomization, distills their action trajectories into latent diffusion, and guides diffusion at inference with differentiable task costs. Combining costs enables fresh waypoint, joystick, obstacle, and motion-inpainting objectives without task-specific RL retraining.
limitations: Guidance relies on tractable differentiable objectives and remains sensitive to data support and modeling errors. Successful G1 demonstrations are task-specific, not proof of arbitrary manipulation or semantic language composition. Per-motion tracking and distilled general policies should be distinguished in comparisons.
method: BeyondMimic trains robust whole-body tracking policies with adaptive motion sampling and sim-to-real randomization, distills their action trajectories into latent diffusion, and guides diffusion at inference with differentiable task costs. Combining costs enables fresh waypoint, joystick, obstacle, and motion-inpainting objectives without task-specific RL retraining.
conditions: Robot proprioception and task commands, optional keyframes, waypoints, or scene obstacles; low-level latent actions generate joint commands. Scene-aware guidance uses environmental localization information, whereas many tracking demonstrations run onboard without external motion capture.
evaluation: The Results section separates scalable tracking from inference-time skill repurposing. Adaptive-sampling ablations compare difficult segments, latent-diffusion ablations test cartwheel sim-to-sim transfer, and real Unitree G1 examples demonstrate selected skills, transitions, and guided tasks.
evidence_locator: Results: Scalable Learning, Versatile Control, Adaptive Sampling and Latent Diffusion ablations; Methods motion tracking/diffusion guidance; supplementary S2/Table S8 and deployment settings.
data_split: Reference motions are drawn from several prior collections, Unitree-retargeted LAFAN1, and animation packs; supplementary Table S8 lists validated motions. No standard human/recording-disjoint train/validation/test ratio is reported. Unseen tasks mean new test-time cost objectives, not necessarily unseen source motion categories.
metrics: Tracking errors measure global/local pose accuracy; motion completion without falling defines cartwheel transfer success. Learning curves and failure rates assess adaptive sampling; task-specific navigation/command errors and hardware rollouts assess guided control. Latency and deployment constraints affect practical feasibility.

title: Retargeting Matters: General Motion Retargeting for Humanoid Motion Tracking
summary: Studies how retargeting quality affects BeyondMimic tracking on LAFAN1 and introduces GMR.
limitations: Trajectory-specific policy success is not zero-shot motion generalization. Sim-to-sim robustness is not a broad real-robot deployment benchmark. Retargeting quality supports composition pipelines but does not demonstrate language-conditioned generation or object-contact preservation.
method: General Motion Retargeting maps human and robot key bodies, aligns rest-pose frames and applies nonuniform local Cartesian scaling. Two inverse-kinematics stages prioritize orientation and then translation/orientation with limits. The paper separately investigates how retargeting artifacts affect independently developed BeyondMimic tracking policies rather than tuning a tracker per retargeter.
conditions: Human BVH/SMPL motion, robot morphology and user-defined key-body correspondence/weights. Outputs robot root/joint trajectories; subsequent RL tracking consumes those references.
evaluation: Each policy receives 100 nominal, 4,096 domain-randomized and 100 ROS/MuJoCo sim-to-sim rollouts. Compares GMR, PHC, ProtoMotions and proprietary Unitree retargets; the study identifies penetration, self-intersection, velocity spikes and initialization sensitivity.
evidence_locator: Sections III.A–III.E, IV (GMR), V; Table I and tracking/user-study result tables.
data_split: Uses twenty-one selected LAFAN1 sequences lasting five seconds to two minutes, excluding most complex non-foot environmental contacts. Trains a separate tracker per trajectory; this is not a conventional training/held-out motion split. User study samples fifteen motions.
metrics: Full-sequence success rate, global/root-relative body-position errors and joint-angle error; user preference for resemblance to the original human clip. Tracking errors are measured while the policy remains alive.

title: Expressive Whole-Body Control for Humanoid Robots
summary: Tracks upper-body expression while lower-body velocity control enables robust locomotion, with real robot demonstrations.
limitations: Leg imitation is deliberately relaxed; root/upper-body reward scores are not full-body reconstruction accuracy. Demonstrated bottle or basketball gestures do not establish contact-rich manipulation. Hardware morphology, torque and limited environmental interaction restrict claims beyond expressive locomotion.
method: Learns expressive humanoid control by separating upper-body imitation goals from root movement commands. Human mocap is retargeted by joint-axis mapping; the lower body is free to maintain balance and locomote instead of copying incompatible leg motion. Reference-state initialization and root-command distributions sampled from real motion guide PPO exploration. Reward terms combine upper-body joint/keypoint tracking, velocity/orientation tracking and regularization.
conditions: Upper-body reference joint/keypoint trajectories, root velocity, roll/pitch/yaw and height commands, plus deployable proprioception. A text-to-motion model may supply references upstream but is separate from the motor policy.
evaluation: Simulation comparison samples 10,000 trajectories across 4,096 environments. Ablations add AMP, remove reference-state initialization, sample random commands or impose full-body tracking. Unitree H1 demonstrations show expressive motion during locomotion.
evidence_locator: Sections II–IV; Tables II–IV; Figures 3–9; data curation, reward and real-world-results paragraphs.
data_split: Trains on 780 selected CMU clips totaling 13,383 seconds, filtering strong object/person/terrain interactions. Table II lists selected real-world test expressions and separate diffusion-generated examples; no random proportional or actor-disjoint split is specified.
metrics: Mean episode length (MEL), linear-velocity tracking reward (MELV), roll/pitch tracking reward (MERP), key-body tracking reward (MEK); distribution plots and real-robot demonstrations supplement these reward-based measures.

title: CFGComposer: Compositional Audio-Text-to-Motion Generation via Copula Score Correction
summary: CFGComposer combines frozen audio-to-motion and text-to-motion diffusion experts, deriving a missing cross-modal score term relative to naive product-of-experts fusion. A jointly trained audio-text denoiser estimates an epsilon-space correction; an inference weight interpolates or amplifies that correction over the composed expert prediction.
limitations: The method is not training-free: a joint model learns the correction. At scale one its defined correction returns the joint prediction algebraically; probabilistic interpretation does not independently prove estimator accuracy. Sparse paired data, validation-only reporting, and whole-body captions limit generalization claims.
method: CFGComposer combines frozen audio-to-motion and text-to-motion diffusion experts, deriving a missing cross-modal score term relative to naive product-of-experts fusion. A jointly trained audio-text denoiser estimates an epsilon-space correction; an inference weight interpolates or amplifies that correction over the composed expert prediction.
conditions: Speech audio encoded with Whisper, a gesture caption, and a framewise gesture-window mask. Five-second clips contain 300 frames and 60 robot joints after G1/BrainCo retargeting. Specified timing is an input, not automatically inferred from unrestricted speech semantics.
evaluation: Table I compares prior AT2M systems; ablations compare naive PoE, finetuning, mixed-data training, and correction-scale sweeps. The operating scale 0.7 is selected using semantic fidelity. A real G1 demonstration supplements automatic and preference evaluation.
evidence_locator: §III inputs, §IV score derivation, §V/Algorithms 1–2 training/inference, §VI.A (775/195 clips), Table I, §VI.C scale ablations and deployment.
data_split: BEAT-derived annotated clips yield 775 training and 195 validation examples after five temporal-offset augmentations per annotation. No separately described held-out test set or speaker/annotation-group split is given in the inspected setup; correlation between offset variants therefore needs checking before reuse.
metrics: G-MSE measures joint error in gesture windows, F-MSE full-clip error, BA audio/motion beat alignment, SRGR semantics-weighted keypoint recall, FID feature-distribution mismatch, and DIV variation. Blind human comparisons assess naturalness, semantic accuracy, beat matching, and diversity.

title: Multi-Modal Controlled Coherent Motion Generation
summary: Combines text, speech and trajectory denoisers by body region and recurrently assembles a holistic motion at each diffusion step.
method: Four modality/component denoisers use body masks; a timeline can reassign parts and an LLM can plan intervals.
conditions: Concurrent speech audio, text intervals and optional trajectory. Four component/modality denoisers assign speech to upper-body/facial detail and text to lower body; holistic assembly repeats each diffusion step, with timeline overrides and optional LLM planning.
evaluation: Table 2 compares Weighted Sum, Pseudo-Text and SynTalker. Since baselines cannot accept asynchronous inputs, their text/audio intervals are synchronized. Additional studies test component assembly, trajectory guidance and control overrides, distinguishing benchmark consistency from broad semantic coverage.
limitations: Default fixed part allocation can conflict when text and speech both control upper-body actions. Curated lower-body text and familiar audio-source evaluation do not establish arbitrary cross-modal generalization, object interaction or physically executed gait.
evidence_locator: Sections 3.1–3.4, 4.1–4.4; Table 2; Appendices E/H and extended user-study tables.
data_split: Text training uses the AMASS portion of HumanML3D in SMPL-X; BEAT2 speakers with IDs below ten supply 10.15 training hours. A 1,000-clip test benchmark combines forty lower-body texts and BEAT2 test audio, each with two texts/two neighboring audio clips.
metrics: Text-side FID+, R1 and TMR M2T/M2M; speech-side FID-A, beat consistency and L1 diversity. Five random five-second crops contribute to FID+; human preference measures coherence, timing and instruction following.

title: Lodge: A Coarse to Fine Diffusion Network for Long Dance Generation Guided by the Characteristic Dance Primitives
summary: Global diffusion generates characteristic dance primitives; parallel local diffusion expands them into detailed long sequences, with a foot refinement component.
limitations: Kinematic FID is a statistical proxy, not physics certification. The method cannot generate detailed hand gestures or facial expressions. Long dance continuity and beat synchronization do not establish object-state dependencies, natural locomotion-to-manipulation transitions or semantic skill holdouts.
method: Uses global diffusion to generate characteristic dance primitives from long music context and local diffusion to expand them into detailed windows in parallel. Hard boundary keymotions connect adjacent windows; soft primitives are mirrored, beat-aligned and choreography-augmented to guide expressive motion. A foot-refinement block operates through forward-kinematics foot features, and a genre discriminator encourages musical-style consistency.
conditions: Music features, dance genre and generated characteristic motion primitives. Optional primitives guide local generation; this is music-conditioned choreography rather than text/object task composition.
evaluation: Compares FACT, MNET, Bailando and EDGE, with ablations on primitives, mirroring, beat alignment, soft cues and foot refinement. Both long FineDance and shorter AIST++ evaluations separate choreography from local motion detail.
evidence_locator: Sections 3.2–3.4, 4.1–4.4 and 5; Tables 1–5; Foot Refine Block and evaluation metric definitions.
data_split: FineDance experiments use 20 music pieces in its test set and generate 1,024-frame/34.13-second samples; reviewed text does not restate full train/validation counts. AIST++ follows Bailando’s protocol, training at 30 FPS and interpolating outputs to 60 FPS for evaluation.
metrics: Kinematic/geometric FID measure motion-feature distribution discrepancy; DIVk/DIVg measure feature variation. Beat Alignment Score measures movement/music synchronization; Foot Skating Ratio counts contact frames with excessive sliding; runtime measures generation efficiency.

summary: EDGE trains a music-conditioned diffusion Transformer with Jukebox audio features and geometric/foot-contact losses. method: EDGE trains a music-conditioned diffusion Transformer with Jukebox audio features and geometric/foot-contact losses. conditions: Music features, requested motion duration, and optional temporal or jointwise constraints. Supplied poses/joints are preserved during denoising; long sequences concatenate overlapping windows. Music-conditioned dance differs from text-ordered locomotion followed by object manipulation.

summary: RealisMotion separates subject appearance, background video, world-space trajectory, and action. A ground-aware coordinate system, focal-length calibration, trajectory unprojection, speed alignment, and orientation adjustment edit 3D motion. Wan-based video diffusion injects subject tokens, background channels, and added motion control signals.
limitations: Estimated depth, camera calibration, body recovery, and 3D-to-video alignment remain error sources. Internal training data limit reproducibility. Visually consistent world-space animation does not establish accurate contact, object dynamics, or robot executability; cross-domain characters are demonstrations rather than comprehensive controlled evaluation.
method: RealisMotion separates subject appearance, background video, world-space trajectory, and action. A ground-aware coordinate system, focal-length calibration, trajectory unprojection, speed alignment, and orientation adjustment edit 3D motion. Wan-based video diffusion injects subject tokens, background channels, and added motion control signals.
conditions: A reference subject image, background video, trajectory and action controls, with optional text/face cues. Actions may come from a motion bank or text-to-motion generator. An image-to-video variant merges subject/background and consequently loses their independent customization.
evaluation: Table 2 compares trajectory control with Wan, Tora, and RealisDance-DiT; Table 3 evaluates action control. Table 4 ablates calibration, body-hand matching, text, extra face input, positional encoding, and random masking. Subject/background customization is largely illustrated qualitatively.
evidence_locator: §3 decomposed 3D editing/video injection; §§4.1–4.3, Tables 2–4; supplementary training details and depth-error robustness analysis.
data_split: Finetunes Wan-2.1 14B on an internal approximately 3,300-hour video collection. Evaluates trajectory/orientation on a newly assembled 100-video Trajectory100 set and action on RealisDance-Val. Exact training/validation partition proportions and source-identity grouping are not reported in the inspected setup.
metrics: Translation error in meters and rotation error in degrees measure recovered trajectory/orientation agreement. PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS assess image fidelity/perception; FID and FVD assess image/video feature-distribution mismatch. These are video-control metrics rather than physical human-object motion scores.
